Hiding What You Can't See

This lesson has now produced three different statuses for "no" — 401, 403, and a scope-driven 404. Here's the rule that decides between them.

Stepping back over everything built so far this lesson, there are now three distinct ways a protected route can refuse a request, and this project draws a deliberate line between them rather than reaching for whichever feels closest:

  • 401 Unauthorized — authenticate (the authentication-middleware topic): there's no valid proof of who this is at all. No token, an expired one, a forged one.
  • 403 Forbidden — authorize('agent', 'admin') (the role-based-authorization topic): this project knows exactly who's asking, and that role is simply never allowed to perform this action, no matter which specific ticket, comment, or tag it's aimed at.
  • 404 Not Found — scopeForViewer (the role-scoped-queries topic): the action itself is something this role can do in general, but this specific row isn't visible to them right now.

That third one is the one worth sitting with, because it's a deliberate choice, not the "obvious" one. An agent PATCHing a ticket in a different agent's queue could, in principle, get a 403 too — "this ticket exists, but it's not yours." This project's getTicketById(id, viewer) (role- scoped-queries topic) doesn't distinguish that case from the ticket genuinely not existing at all — both resolve to null, and both produce the identical 404. The reasoning: revealing "this exists, you're just not allowed to touch it" is itself a small leak of information about data this viewer has no visibility into — how many tickets exist, which ids are in use, that someone has claimed this one. Treating "not yours" and "doesn't exist" as indistinguishable closes that leak entirely, at the cost of a slightly less specific error message for a legitimate agent who just mistyped an id.
